lines.text: Founded by freed American slaves, Africa's first republic lived through a long elite rule, two brutal wars and a hard-won peace. This is the story of Liberia.
Joseph Jenkins Roberts, born free in Virginia in 1809, would sail to Africa and become the country's first president.
In 1816, Americans founded the Colonization Society, to send freed black Americans to settle in West Africa.
In 1822, the first settlers landed on the coast, and Liberia, the land of the free, was begun.
They founded Monrovia, named after the American president James Monroe. It is the capital still.
William Tubman, born in 1895, would rule as president for twenty-seven years.
From 1926, the American tyre maker Firestone ran the largest rubber plantation in the world here, shaping the country's economy.
Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, born in 1938, would become the first woman elected to lead an African country.
Joseph Boakai, born in 1944, would become president in 2024.
Charles Taylor, born in 1948, would become a warlord, then president, and later be convicted of war crimes in Sierra Leone.
In 1980, a soldier named Samuel Doe seized power, ending more than a century of rule by the settlers' descendants. He was killed in 1990.
George Weah, from the slums of Monrovia, would become the only African to win the Ballon d'Or, and later president.
Leymah Gbowee would lead a movement of women that helped end the war, and win the Nobel Peace Prize.
In 1989, Liberia fell into civil war. For eight years, fighting tore through the country.
Two years after it ended, war came again in 1999. By 2003, the two wars had killed some quarter of a million people.
Peace came, but in 2014 Ebola struck. The largest outbreak ever swept through Liberia, and many health workers gave their lives.
From the first settlers' landing to peace after war, Liberia keeps building its republic.
